opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it changes things quite a bit. When we started doing AI service cards at AWS, we were mostly dealing with what I'd call narrow or task-specific services: face matching, speech-to-text, text extraction from documents. For those, you can be fairly precise about the intended use case. You can say, here's what the service is designed to do, here are the inputs it expects, here's how we measured accuracy, and here's how performance varies across demographic groups or acoustic conditions or whatever the relevant dimensions are. The evaluation problem, while not trivial, is reasonably well defined, because the output is something like a similarity score or a transcription that you can check against ground truth.

Generative AI breaks a lot of that. First, the use cases are open-ended. A large language model or an image generator isn't built for one task; customers will use it for summarization, code generation, customer service, creative writing, and things we never anticipated. So the idea of documenting the intended use becomes much fuzzier, and you have to think harder about how to communicate what the system is good at and where it shouldn't be relied on.

Second, the notion of correctness gets slippery. For a transcription, there's a right answer. For "write me a paragraph about this topic," there are many acceptable answers and many subtly bad ones. So evaluation shifts from simple accuracy metrics toward a much broader set of concerns: hallucinations or factual errors, toxicity, the potential to reproduce copyrighted material, privacy leakage, robustness to adversarial prompting and jailbreaks. Each of those is its own research area, and in several of them the science of measurement is still pretty immature.

Third, fairness itself becomes harder to even define. With a classifier, you can talk about error rates across groups. With a generative model, you're asking things like: does it produce stereotyped content when prompted about certain groups, does its quality degrade for certain dialects or languages? Those are real questions, but turning them into crisp, reportable numbers is much harder.

And finally, there's the shared-responsibility aspect, which was always there but is amplified now. The provider builds the foundation model, but the customer chooses the prompts, fine-tunes it, adds guardrails, and deploys it in a specific context. So a service card for a generative model has to be very clear that the provider's evaluations are a starting point, and that customers need to do their own testing on their own use case. In some sense the card becomes less a statement of "here's how well this works" and more a guide to "here's what we tested, here's what we know, here are the risks, and here's how you should think about evaluating it for yourself."

So I'd say the core goal, transparency about capabilities and limitations, stays the same, but the content and the methodology behind it have to evolve substantially, and honestly, the field is still figuring that out.

r001.rationale: The response says generative outputs can have hallucinations or factual errors and contrasts their evaluation with simple accuracy metrics, but it does not distinguish hallucinations from ordinary classifier errors such as false positives or false negatives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a great question, and I think it really gets at the heart of what's changed for us. So let me back up a little bit. When we started doing service cards at AWS, the sort of canonical example was something like Rekognition face matching. And what's nice about a service like that, from a documentation and a responsible AI perspective, is that it's a very well-defined task. You've got two images, you want to know whether they're the same person, there's a right answer, and so you can talk very concretely about things like intended use cases, you can measure accuracy, you can slice that accuracy across demographic groups, you can say here's where we've tested it and here's where we haven't. The space of things people might do with it is relatively bounded.

Generative AI just blows that up. With a large language model, there isn't a single task. The task is whatever the user types into the box. So the first challenge is just, what does "intended use" even mean when the intended use is essentially open-ended? You can't enumerate it. And relatedly, what does it mean to evaluate the thing? With face matching I can give you an error rate. With a model that can write code, summarize documents, translate, role-play, give you medical information it shouldn't, there's no single number, and frankly there's no finite set of numbers that fully characterizes it. So we've had to shift from thinking about performance on a task to thinking about properties of the model more broadly, things like truthfulness, toxicity, robustness to adversarial prompting, fairness across many different kinds of uses, and be honest about the fact that our evaluations are necessarily a sample from an enormous space.

The second big change is that the failure modes are qualitatively different. In the classical setting, the failure is basically a wrong answer. In the generative setting, you've got hallucination, which is the model confidently making things up, you've got the model being manipulated through the prompt into doing things the developer didn't intend, you've got the fact that the output is itself something that goes out into the world and can cause harm in ways that are hard to anticipate. So the service card has to talk much more about limitations and about what the developer building on top of the model is responsible for, because a lot of the mitigation has to happen at the application layer, not the model layer.

And then I'd say the third thing is more of a process challenge. These models are moving incredibly fast. The traditional model card was sort of a static artifact, you train the thing, you evaluate it, you write it up. Now you've got models being updated frequently, you've got fine-tuning, you've got retrieval, you've got agents chaining calls together, and the documentation has to keep up with that. So we've been thinking about the service card less as a document and more as part of an ongoing practice, where you're continually probing the model, red-teaming it, and updating what you tell people.

I'll say one more thing, which is that in some ways I think this has made the cards more important, not less. When the model was narrow, a sophisticated customer could probably figure out its limitations on their own. With these general models, even the people who built them don't fully understand their behavior, so being transparent about what we know, what we don't know, and how we tested, is really the best we can offer, and I think it's incumbent on us to do that well.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a conventional system’s basic wrong-answer failure with generative hallucination, where the model confidently makes things up.

astra-6.text:
I think generative AI makes the challenge considerably harder, because the range of things a system can do is so much broader. If you have a model whose job is to predict whether a transaction is fraudulent, you have a fairly well-defined task. You can ask about its accuracy, the kinds of errors it makes, and how those errors vary across populations.

With a generative model, users can ask for things that the developers never anticipated. So what would it mean to give a comprehensive account of that system’s limitations? You can evaluate it on particular tasks, but that doesn’t establish how it will behave across all of those possible uses.

That makes it especially important for a service card to distinguish what has actually been tested from what remains unknown. And the context matters: the underlying model is one thing; a service built around it, with particular data, safeguards, and users, is another. I think these cards have to become living documents, updated as the system changes and as we learn more about how people use it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions conventional classifier errors and generative-model limitations, but it does not distinguish hallucinations from ordinary prediction errors such as false positives or false negatives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generative AI makes the challenge considerably harder, because the range of things a system can do—and the range of ways people can use it—is so broad. If you’re building a model for a fairly specific prediction task, you can describe that task, identify relevant measures of performance, and ask how those measures vary across populations. Those are already difficult questions, but at least you have a reasonably well-defined target.

With a generative model, somebody can come along with a prompt or an application that you never anticipated. So what would it mean for a service card to comprehensively describe its behavior? You can evaluate particular capabilities and particular risks, but you have to be careful about suggesting that those evaluations cover every possible use.

That makes the distinction between the underlying model and the service built around it especially important. The same model can behave quite differently depending on the instructions, the data it has access to, and the safeguards in the application. I think these cards will need to be more specific about the conditions under which claims were tested, more explicit about uncertainty, and updated as we learn from actual use.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts generative models with specific prediction tasks, but does not distinguish hallucination from a conventional classifier error such as a false positive or false negative.
